d.title: Four cases, and in each one `__init__` runs too late
d.caption: **You will write `__init__` constantly and `__new__` perhaps twice in a career — it exists for the cases where you must control *which object is returned*, not merely how it is populated.** The first row is the clearest: **subclassing an immutable type fixes the value at allocation, so by the time `__init__` runs it is too late to change.** And the two middle rows share one reason: **`__init__` cannot choose to return a different object**, so caching, interning and singletons are all out of its reach.

state: the value is fixed at allocation

d.title: Five options, and the first one covers most code
d.caption: **A function, for one behaviour with no state between calls — which is most code.** The two middle rows are where records belong: **a dataclass is the modern default for data with a few fields and little behaviour, and a NamedTuple when the record should behave like a tuple.** A class earns its place when there is **state plus several methods that operate on it, or a type you will subclass or substitute.** And the row people forget: **a module is already a namespace of related functions with no per-instance state.**

items.label: A function
items.sub: one behaviour, no state between calls

items.label: A dataclass
items.sub: a few fields, little behaviour - the modern default

items.label: A NamedTuple
items.sub: an immutable record that behaves like a tuple

items.label: A class
items.sub: state plus several methods, or a type to substitute

d.title: The same name gives a function off the class and a bound method off the instance
d.caption: **A method is just a class attribute that happens to be a function — `Order.total` is a plain function and `order.total` is a bound method, and `order.total.__func__ is Order.total` is `True`.** Which explains the last two rows, and they are the practical consequence: **assigning to an instance attribute shadows the class attribute for that instance only**, so `order.discount = 999` leaves every other instance reading the class value of 100. **The lookup is instance dict first, then the class** — and nothing warns you that you have shadowed a method.

d.title: 152 bytes to 56, and the object can no longer grow an attribute
d.caption: **`__slots__` removes the per-instance `__dict__` — 152 bytes becomes 56, a 2.7× reduction — and the trade is in the next two rows.** `hasattr(obj, "__dict__")` is now `False`, **so assigning an attribute the class did not declare raises `AttributeError` instead of silently creating one.** Which is a feature for a data class and a problem for anything that patches attributes on at runtime: **a mixin, a cache attribute, `functools.cached_property` and most ORM instrumentation all need the dict that slots removed.**

d.title: Six reasons given for a staticmethod, and three of them hold
d.caption: **A `staticmethod` receives neither the instance nor the class — it is a plain function that happens to live inside a class body — so the honest question is always: why is it in the class?** The three weak answers all have the same cheaper alternative: **namespacing by module is cheaper and more discoverable, and a module-level `_helper` says “only this class uses it” without the coupling.** The legitimate three are different in kind: **two are constraints you did not choose, and one is a genuine public check — `Order.is_valid_amount(x)` reads well.**

columns.title: Weak — use a module instead
items: 'it is related to this class'
'it is a helper only this class uses'
'it belongs on the class for organisation'
and all three make the class harder to test in isolation

columns.title: Legitimate
items: 'subclasses need to override it' — though that is probably a classmethod
'existing code calls it through the instance' — a constraint you did not choose
'it is a validator the class exposes' — Order.is_valid_amount(x) reads well

d.title: A bound method carries its instance, which is why a callback keeps the object alive
d.caption: **`obj.send` is a bound method: it holds a reference to `obj`, so `obj.send.__self__ is obj` is `True` and `obj.send.__func__` is the plain function.** The consequence is the one that matters in long-lived code: **passing `obj.send` as a callback stores a reference to the whole object, so a registry of callbacks keeps every instance alive** — which is a memory leak that looks like a list of functions. **`weakref.WeakMethod` is the fix when the registry should not own the object.**

d.title: A registry whose error message lists what it has
d.caption: **`classmethod` is what makes a registry work, because the subclass registering itself needs to know *which* class it is** — `__init_subclass__` or an explicit `register` both hand you `cls`. The output is the part worth copying: **`ValueError: no exporter for 'xml'; have ['csv', 'json']`.** A lookup that fails with just `KeyError: 'xml'` makes the caller go and read the registry; **this one answers the next question in the message**, which costs one f-string and saves a round trip in every bug report.

d.title: A getter with no setter is as close as Python gets to a read-only field
d.caption: **No setter means assignment raises `AttributeError` — and that is enough**, because the point is to stop accidental writes rather than to make them impossible. `cached_property` goes further: **it replaces itself with the computed value in the instance `__dict__` on first access**, so the second read is a plain attribute lookup. Which creates the failure the lesson measures: **on mutable state it goes stale — the cache has no idea the fields it read have changed**, so it belongs on immutable objects or needs explicit invalidation.

nodes.label: cached_property writes into __dict__
nodes.sub: first access computes, then it is gone

nodes.label: So on mutable state it goes stale
nodes.sub: it cannot know the fields changed

d.title: Five tests, and each one is about what the caller will assume
d.caption: The rule behind all five: **a property makes a call look like an attribute read, so the caller will treat it like one — cheap, repeatable, side-effect free.** Break any of those and the syntax is lying. **The clearest violation is a property that does I/O: `order.customer` that silently issues a database query looks free at the call site, and in a loop it is N queries nobody wrote.** And the last row is the one that catches people: **`next_id` as a property that increments a counter is a method wearing attribute syntax.**

columns.title: A property
items: conceptually an attribute — a value the object has
cheap: no I/O, no significant computation
no side effects
takes no arguments
repeated access is safe and idempotent

columns.title: A method
items: an action the object performs
does I/O, or takes measurable time
changes state, writes, or sends something
needs arguments
calling it twice differs from calling it once

d.title: Reusing code is the most common reason people inherit wrongly
d.caption: **Inheritance says a `Child` is usable anywhere a `Parent` is expected. If that is not true, you want composition** — and the measured output is the test passing: the subclass answers the base's call and `isinstance` is `True`. The sentence to keep is the negative one: **reusing code is not a reason to inherit.** A subclass that inherits only to borrow three helper methods **has bought substitutability it does not want and cannot honour**, and every caller that relies on the base's contract is now relying on something untrue.

d.title: C3 refuses rather than guessing, and the error names the bases
d.caption: **`TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases X, Y` — raised at class *definition* time, not at a call.** Which is the good news in this section: **the one inheritance mistake Python catches for you is an impossible linearisation**, because C3 requires that each base's own order is preserved and that a class precedes its parents. **Two hierarchies that disagree about the order of X and Y cannot both be honoured, so it refuses rather than picking one** — and the fix is always to make the orders agree.

steps.code: class Z(X, Y) with conflicting orders

state: consistent MRO for bases X, Y

d.title: A mixin that behaves assumes nothing and calls `super()`
d.caption: The measured output shows both working: **a mixin adding `to_json` produces `{"name": "deploy", "priority": 2}` without knowing what class it is mixed into.** The rules that make that true are short. **Name methods so they cannot collide, assume no attributes you did not declare, and always call `super()` so the next class in the MRO still runs.** A mixin that reads `self.name` without declaring it **works until it is mixed into something without a name**, and the failure is an `AttributeError` far from the mixin.

d.title: The contract becomes visible without anyone inheriting anything
d.caption: **Duck typing's weakness is that the contract is invisible — `alert_all(notifiers, ...)` does not say what a notifier is, so a wrong object fails at the call, at runtime, possibly in production.** `Protocol` fixes that without giving up the freedom: **the consumer writes down the methods it needs, providers satisfy it structurally without importing or inheriting anything, and mypy checks the match.** Which is the whole trade: **you get a checkable contract and you need a type checker in CI for it to mean anything at all.**

nodes.label: Duck typing: the contract is invisible
nodes.sub: a wrong object fails at the call

nodes.label: The CONSUMER declares what it needs
nodes.sub: a Protocol, in its own module

nodes.label: Without a checker in CI it is a comment

d.title: A string passed where a list of strings was meant, and no error anywhere
d.caption: **No error, because `str` genuinely is iterable — it just iterates at the wrong granularity.** This is the canonical failure of duck typing: **the object has the right shape and the wrong meaning**, so every structural check passes and the behaviour is wrong. The defences are worth taking in order: **a `list[str]` hint so mypy catches it, an explicit `isinstance(recipients, str)` guard at any public boundary, and a signature that takes the single case separately** — because the shape cannot distinguish them.

state: the shape cannot tell them apart

d.title: Three plausible is-a claims, and only one of them is a good idea
d.caption: **The usual advice — inherit when B is-a A, compose when B has-a A — is correct and insufficient, because English lets you claim is-a for almost anything.** `AdminUser` is-a `User`. `CachedRepository` is-a `Repository`. `RetryingHttpClient` is-a `HttpClient`. **All plausible, and only one of them is a good idea** — and the test that separates them is not grammatical: **does every caller of the base still get what the base promised, without knowing which subclass it has?** A cache that returns stale data and a client that retries a non-idempotent write both fail it.

nodes.label: CachedRepository is-a Repository
nodes.sub: but it may return stale data

nodes.label: RetryingHttpClient is-a HttpClient
nodes.sub: but it may repeat a write

nodes.label: The real test is not grammar
Does the base's promise still hold?

d.title: Five tests, and two of them are about who controls the code
d.caption: **The first row is the only one that is about correctness and the rest are about change.** Composition wins whenever **behaviour varies along more than one axis**, because inheritance forces you to pick one axis for the hierarchy and encode the rest as classes-per-combination. And the last two rows are the practical ones: **inheritance assumes the relationship will never change for an instance, and that you control both the base and every subclass** — so **wrapping something you do not control is composition by definition.**

columns.title: Inheritance
items: the subclass is genuinely substitutable
a framework requires it — a Django model, a pytest plugin
real shared implementation, one level deep
the relationship never changes for an instance
you control the base and every subclass

columns.title: Composition
items: behaviour varies along more than one axis
you choose the behaviour at runtime or from config
each piece should be testable on its own
the relationship might change during its life
you are wrapping something you do not control

d.title: Who declares the interface is the difference that decides it
d.caption: **An ABC is declared by the provider hierarchy and a Protocol by the consumer that needs it** — and every other row follows from that. **Providers must inherit from an ABC, which is real coupling and impossible for third-party classes**; a Protocol is satisfied structurally, so it works on classes you cannot modify. What an ABC buys for that cost is genuine: **shared concrete implementation and state, plus a refusal to instantiate an incomplete subclass at runtime.** A Protocol offers neither — **`isinstance` works only with `@runtime_checkable`, and then it checks names only.**

columns.title: ABC
items: declared by the PROVIDER hierarchy
providers must inherit — real coupling
refuses to instantiate if incomplete, at runtime
can carry concrete methods and state
third-party classes only via register()

columns.title: Protocol
items: declared by the CONSUMER that needs it
satisfied structurally — no inheritance
no runtime enforcement at all
default method bodies only, no state
works on classes you cannot modify

d.title: Three methods written, and the rest arrive free
d.caption: **Inheriting `collections.abc.Mapping` and writing `__getitem__`, `__iter__` and `__len__` gives you `keys`, `values`, `items`, `get`, `__contains__`, `__eq__` and `__ne__`** — which is the case where an ABC's shared implementation is unambiguously worth the coupling. The output shows the derived methods working on a class that never defined them. **And it is the one place to prefer an ABC over a Protocol without hesitation: the standard library's ABCs exist to give you implementation, not just to require methods.**

d.title: register() makes isinstance say yes and changes nothing else
d.caption: **`MyClass` registered against an ABC reports `True` for `isinstance` and `issubclass` — and gains none of the ABC's concrete methods, and is checked for nothing.** Which is the problem: **the claim is now a lie that the runtime agrees with.** A class registered as a `Mapping` that lacks `keys` passes every `isinstance` guard and fails at the first call. **So `register()` buys a true-looking answer to the wrong question**, and the honest alternative is a `Protocol`, which checks the shape it actually needs.

nodes.label: So a missing method passes the guard
Use a Protocol instead
nodes.sub: it checks the shape you need

d.title: One abstract method, one implementation, no state — that is a function
d.caption: **An ABC with a single abstract method, whose subclasses hold no state and share no implementation, is a function with extra ceremony.** The test is mechanical: **if every subclass is `def run(self, x): return ...` and nothing reads `self`, the hierarchy is carrying nothing.** Which is 3.4's point arriving from the other direction — **the interface is the call signature** — and the replacement is a dict of functions or a `Callable` hint. **The ABC earns its place the moment a subclass needs state, configuration, or a second related method.**

nodes.label: Use a function, or a Callable hint
It earns it back with state

d.title: One `__lt__` plus a decorator, and 1.10.0 sorts after 1.2.5
d.caption: **`functools.total_ordering` derives the other five comparisons from `__lt__` and `__eq__`** — so one method gives you sorting, `max`, `min` and the full set of operators. The output is the point of having it at all: **`[Version(1,2,0), Version(1,2,5), Version(1,10,0)]`, where string comparison would have put `1.10.0` before `1.2.0`** because `'1'` sorts before `'2'`. And the dataclass alternative is worth knowing: **`order=True` generates the same four from field order**, which is right only when the natural sort really is field order.

d.title: Five methods, and the object works with nine built-in constructs
d.caption: **Write `__len__`, `__contains__`, `__getitem__`, `__iter__` and `__bool__` and the object works with `len`, `in`, subscripting, `for`, comprehensions, `sorted`, `sum`, unpacking and truthiness** — which is what “protocol” means operationally. The legacy row is worth knowing because it explains surprising behaviour: **`__getitem__` alone makes an object iterable**, since `for` falls back to calling it with 0, 1, 2 … until `IndexError`. **So a class with only `__getitem__` iterates, and a bug in it becomes an infinite loop.**

state: an infinite loop, via the fallback

d.title: `__exit__`'s return value decides whether the exception survives
d.caption: **`__exit__` receives the exception if one occurred, and its return value decides whether to suppress it — returning `True` swallows the exception, which is almost never what you want.** The trap is that **a bare `return` or a forgotten one returns `None`, which is falsy and therefore correct** — so the dangerous version is the one that accidentally returns something truthy. And on operator overloading: **`__add__` and friends are excellent for genuine mathematical or quantity types and actively harmful elsewhere**, because `order1 + order2` has no obvious meaning.

nodes.label: Return None -> it propagates
nodes.sub: which a bare return gives you

d.title: The dataclass refuses the mutable default rather than sharing it
d.caption: **`ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field items is not allowed: use default_factory`** — raised at class definition, which makes this **the one place Python catches 1.4's shared-mutable-default bug for you.** `field(default_factory=list)` calls the factory per instance. The second output shows the rest of what `field` does: **a generated id, a timestamp, a computed duration and a derived slug**, all set without the caller passing anything — and **`field(init=False)` is what keeps the derived ones out of the signature.**

state: slug, derived - not in the signature

d.title: Four options, and `frozen=True` is the one to reach for by default
d.caption: **`frozen=True` blocks assignment and adds `__hash__`, which is what makes a value object usable as a dict key, a set member, or a shared default** — the measured output puts a `Point` in a set and raises `FrozenInstanceError` on assignment. The others are narrower: **`slots=True` for millions of instances (4.2's 152→56 bytes), `order=True` only when the natural sort really is field order, and `kw_only=True` past two or three fields** — which is 3.2's keyword-only argument arriving as one flag.

only if that IS the sort

d.title: `__post_init__` is where a dataclass gets its invariant
d.caption: **A generated `__init__` assigns the fields and validates nothing — `__post_init__` runs immediately afterwards and is the only hook you get.** So it does two jobs: **compute derived values from the fields that were passed, and enforce the invariant that 4.1 said `__init__` exists for.** The measured output is both: **a duration of 30 computed from two dates, and `ValueError: end 2024-01-01 is before start 2024-01-01` when they are wrong.** On a `frozen=True` dataclass, **assigning a derived field needs `object.__setattr__`.**

and it is the only hook

d.title: A reason to change is a person who might ask for something different
d.caption: **The usual phrasing — *a class should do one thing* — is unfalsifiable, because “one thing” can be any size.** The useful phrasing is **a module should have one reason to change, where a reason is a person or a team who might ask for something different.** Which turns the principle into a question you can answer: **if finance asks for a new tax rule and marketing asks for a new email template, and both land in the same file, that file has two reasons to change** — and the split follows the askers rather than the nouns.

d.title: The principle Python needs most, because nothing checks it
d.caption: **Liskov substitution says a subclass must be usable anywhere its base is, without callers knowing — and this is the principle Python needs most, because nothing checks it: no compiler, no interface declaration, and duck typing means a wrong substitution often runs successfully and produces wrong behaviour.** The Python-specific violation is the one that bites: **a subclass that returns `None` where the base raised, or raises where the base returned a default.** Both satisfy every structural check and every `Protocol`, **because the difference is in what happens on a miss, which no type expresses.**

nodes.label: A subclass must be usable as the base
The Python case: None where the base raised
Every structural check passes
nodes.sub: the difference is in the miss

d.title: Segregation is the default when the consumer declares the interface
d.caption: ***No client should depend on methods it does not use.* In Java this means splitting a fat interface into several — an explicit refactor somebody has to do.** In Python, **because a `Protocol` is declared by the consumer, segregation is the default rather than an effort**: a function that needs one method declares a protocol with one method, and the provider never knows. **So the principle is not something you apply here; it is a consequence of where the declaration lives**, which is 4.8's row about who declares the interface doing real work.

nodes.label: So it is a consequence, not a practice

d.title: Both survive, and what shrinks is the ceremony
d.caption: **Adapter survives because third-party interfaces are a permanent fact — what shrinks is the declaration: no `Target` interface, because a `Protocol` describes what the consumer needs without anybody implementing it.** Proxy survives for **lazy loading, access control and instrumentation, and `__getattr__` makes it cheap** — with one caveat worth knowing before you ship it: **special methods are looked up on the *type*, not the instance, so `__getattr__` never sees `len(proxy)` or `proxy[0]`** and those have to be forwarded explicitly.

items: reshape an interface you do not control
survives: third-party interfaces are permanent
shrinks: no Target interface to declare
a Protocol says what the consumer needs

columns.title: Proxy
items: same interface, added behaviour
survives: lazy loading, access control, instrumentation
shrinks: __getattr__ forwards everything
caveat: special methods are found on the TYPE, so forward them by hand
